title: Relationship between crystallographic texture and anisotropy of tensile properties in a high strength TRIP steel
abstract: The relationship between the crystallographic texture of ferrite and austenite phases with the mechanical anisotropy in a high-strength TRIP steel was studied. The TRIP1100 steel was produced by cold-rolling, intercritical annealing (IA), and subsequent salt bath annealing of a hot-rolled plate. Microstructural investigations utilizing scanning electron microscopy and electron backscatter diffraction revealed that the TRIP steel consisted of ferrite, bainite, retained austenite (RA), and martensite. Recrystallization of ferrite during the IA and transformation of austenite to bainite and martensite during the subsequent salt bath annealing resulted in the formation of moderate α and γ fibers texture in the bcc phase, while a strong brass component resulted from the previous hot-rolling was detected for the RA. Tensile testing along rolling direction (RD), transverse direction, and diagonal direction revealed that the lowest value for the yield stress and the highest value for the initial work-hardening rate is in the RD. The former resulted from the higher area fraction of the ferrite grains with Schmid factor (SF) values above 0.45 for the main slip system of ferrite in the RD, while the latter is due to the lower stability of the RA as a result of a higher area fraction of austenite grains with SF values above 0.44 in the RD. Nevertheless, the TRIP1100 steel exhibited a r-value of 0.927 and a Δr value of 0.005, suggesting a low anisotropy. It can be concluded that the mechanical anisotropy of the TRIP steel is strongly dependent on the texture of both ferrite and RA phases.
